planting.note: Set out container-grown nursery stock in spring into humid, acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil sheltered from wind, ideally with morning sun and afternoon shade.

directions: Set out container-grown nursery stock in spring into humid, acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil sheltered from wind, ideally with morning sun and afternoon shade. True star anise is a slow, long-lived subtropical evergreen native to southern China and northern Vietnam that needs six to eight years of consistent warmth and humidity before it forms its first harvestable star-shaped seed pods. Pods are picked while still green, then sun-dried until they turn the familiar deep reddish-brown, and are essential to Chinese five-spice powder, pho broth, and mulled wine. Do not confuse it with the toxic ornamental anise relatives (Illicium floridanum, I. anisatum) sold for landscaping — only I. verum pods are safe to eat.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, and keep soil consistently moist through the tree's slow multi-year establishment; both male and female trees are needed for fruit.

directions: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade, and keep soil consistently moist through the tree's slow multi-year establishment. Kokum is dioecious, so both male and female trees are needed for fruit, and it is native to the moist forests of India's Western Ghats. The purple-rind fruit is sun-dried into the deep reddish-black souring spice used throughout Goan and Konkani cooking, such as kokum curry and solkadhi, and pressed into kokum butter; fresh pulp is also boiled into a tart, cooling summer syrup.
sources: Kew Science (Plants of the World Online)

planting.note: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into loamy, well-drained soil with a near-neutral pH, in full sun to partial shade; established trees tolerate brief light frost better than true tropical cinnamon relatives.

directions: Transplant container-grown trees in spring into loamy, well-drained soil with a near-neutral pH, in full sun to partial shade; established trees tolerate brief light frost better than true tropical cinnamon relatives. The glossy, distinctly three-veined leaves carry a warm cassia-cinnamon-clove aroma entirely different from true bay laurel and are picked and sun-dried once the tree is a few years established. Tejpat is essential to North Indian garam masala, biryani, and dal tadka, and should not be substituted with Mediterranean bay leaf, which lacks its cinnamon character.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this thorny, deciduous, high-elevation Himalayan relative of Sichuan pepper is markedly more cold-hardy than its lowland cousins.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this thorny, deciduous, high-elevation Himalayan relative of Sichuan pepper is markedly more cold-hardy than its lowland cousins, tolerating winters at elevation across Nepal and northern India. The dried, husked berries deliver an intense citrus-grapefruit aroma alongside the characteristic tongue-tingling numbness of the genus, and are ground fresh for Nepali achar, momo dipping sauces, and spice blends. Harvest ripe berry clusters in autumn and dry them whole before grinding just before use to preserve the volatile citrus notes.
sources: International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD)

planting.note: Nick or soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to break the hard seed coat, then direct-sow shallowly into well-drained sandy or gravelly soil in full sun once the site is frost-free.

directions: Nick or soak seed in freshly boiled water overnight to break the hard seed coat, then direct-sow shallowly into well-drained sandy or gravelly soil in full sun once the site is frost-free; this arid-zone Australian shrub tolerates drought, poor soil, and salinity once established. The ripe, dried seed pods are harvested, roasted, and ground into wattleseed, an Aboriginal bushfood staple with a nutty, roasted-coffee, caramel flavor used to season breads, ice cream, and native spice blends. Prune lightly after seed harvest to maintain a manageable shrub form and encourage a fuller next season's pod set.
